newsitem.title: SPAIN: Aznar travels to Bonn with Maastricht in briefcase.
newsitem.headline: Aznar travels to Bonn with Maastricht in briefcase.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar will travel to Bonn on Thursday determined to persuade a reluctant Germany and its Chancellor Helmut Kohl that Spain should help launch Europe's single currency in 1999.

Armed with a briefcase chock full of his young government's economic accomplishments, Aznar plans to press home Spain's claim to be a founding member of the Euro at the Spanish-German summit to be held in Bonn on Thursday.
It is the first such summit since Aznar's conservative Popular Party took over the government last spring.

"Maastricht will be one of the main themes of the summit and the executive will point out in Bonn his commitment to be in monetary union and to meet the convergence criteria," according to a source in the Spanish delegation.
Aznar will be bringing data detailing the government's feverish clean-up of the Spanish economy, he said.
In 1996, Spain managed to reduce its budget deficit to 4.4 percent of gross domestic product as planned, and the government has said it is convinced it will drop to 3.0 percent this year.
Heartened by the government's grit, markets surged.

Stocks jumped. Bonds far outstripped their German counterparts, with the yield spread - a measure of the added risk of holding Spanish debt -- imploding to around 90 basis points now from 330 in March and 500 in the summer of 1995.
Inflation fell and the peseta, victim of a series of devaluations until March 1995, stabilised near 84.00 per mark.

Now clearly within reach of the economic requirements for the single currency and flush with the accomplishment, Spain has eagerly pushed major European allies for recognition. But so far, Germany appears to have turned a deaf ear.
According to German diplomatic sources, now isn't the right time to discuss the future composition of the single currency.
On Tuesday, Juergen Stark, State Secretary at the Finance Ministry, showed Aznar just how difficult his task will be.
Germany, fearful of losing the solidity of the mark, and haunted by severe bouts of hyperinflation at home earlier this century, may well look askance at the peseta's past turmoil.
"There are members whose economic structures are not yet well enough prepared to take part," Stark said.
Even some countries who qualify on paper "would be well advised to maintain exchange rate flexibility for a certain period," he said.
Spain may well feel deflated that its efforts fail to move Germany, but according to German diplomatic sources the timing is premature and Kohl is unlikely to provide any assurances.
Germany will instead keep to its policy that members for the single currency will be chosen in the spring of 1998 based on economic data for 1997.
In addition, Germany is in no position to sit in judgment of Spain's performance given its public deficit running at 3.9 percent, German diplomatic sources said.
